paper_title: MMFlash: Faster Speculative Decoding for Vision-Language Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Speculative decoding accelerates generation by letting a lightweight drafter propose tokens for parallel verification by a target model. Diffusion drafters such as DFlash propose an entire token block in a single forward pass, but mainly focus on text-only tasks, leaving multimodal drafting underexplored. To study this setting, we first introduce a metric of token-level visual dependence based on the KL divergence between next-token distributions with and without visual input. We find that acceptance rates decrease from 46% in the lowest visual-dependence quartile to 22% in the highest, with this disparity persisting after multimodal training. Motivated by this observation, we propose MMFlash, a simple and effective framework that adaptively upweights visually dependent tokens that the drafter predicts poorly. For long video inputs, MMFlash further employs sparse attention to reduce redundant attention computation and improve drafting quality. Across various multimodal benchmarks, MMFlash achieves lossless decoding speedups of up to $3.58\times$, outperforming EAGLE-3 and DFlash by up to 195.4% and 17.1%, respectively.

sections.content: Speculative decoding accelerates generation by letting lightweight drafter propose tokens for parallel verification by target model. Diffusion drafters such as DFlash propose an entire token block in single forward pass, but mainly focus on text-only tasks, leaving multimodal drafting underexplored. To study this setting, we first introduce metric of token-level visual dependence based on the KL divergence between next-token distributions with and without visual input. We find that acceptance rates decrease from 46% in the lowest visual-dependence quartile to 22% in the highest, with this disparity persisting after multimodal training. Motivated by this observation, we propose MMFlash, simple and effective framework that adaptively upweights visually dependent tokens that the drafter predicts poorly. For long video inputs, MMFlash further employs sparse attention to reduce redundant attention computation and improve drafting quality. Across various multimodal benchmarks, MMFlash achieves lossless decoding speedups of up to 3.58, outperforming EAGLE-3 and DFlash by up to 195.4% and 17.1%, respectively. 1. Introduction Vision-language models (VLMs) [1, 4, 58, 62] have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across multimodal tasks such as visual question answering (VQA) [2, 61, 72], video understanding [15, 36, 64], and visual reasoning [11, 12, 45, 69]. However, their inference efficiency remains constrained by autoregressive generation, which produces tokens sequentially. This bottleneck is further exacerbated by the growing adoption of reasoning models that generate longer responses [10, 19, 25]. Speculative decoding [6, 34, 66] has emerged as prominent solution: small model drafts multiple tokens, which larger target model then verifies in parallel, substantially accelerating decoding. *Corresponding author. Figure 1. Decoding speedup comparison with SOTA speculative decoding methods (EAGLE-3 & DFlash) on SGLang. The performance of speculative decoding largely depends on draft quality and drafting cost. Early approaches include Medusa [5], which augments the target model with multiple decoding heads, and the EAGLE series [37 39, 57], which drafts from target model features and uses tree-based verification to increase acceptance lengths. For autoregressive drafters, however, each drafting step requires forward pass, making drafting cost grow linearly with draft length. This favors lightweight architectures, often at the expense of draft quality. Inspired by diffusion language models (DLMs) [9, 49, 71], recent methods [23, 42, 65, 73] such as DFlash [7] use block diffusion [3] to generate an entire draft block in single forward pass, decoupling the number of sequential drafting steps from the number of proposed tokens. The computational budget previously spent on repeated sequential passes can thus support deeper, higher-capacity drafters, improving draft quality. Building on these advances, we extend diffusion drafting to multimodal models, direction that remains largely unexplored. To better extend to the vision field, we first introduce 1 Figure 2. Overview of MMFlash. (a) The target VLM is run twice on the same prefix x<t, with and without the image I, and the visual dependence score dt is the KL divergence between the two next-token distributions. Each masked position of block keeps its base weight bk and gains visual bonus that depends on dt. (b) The MMFlash drafter adopts simple sparse attention pattern for video inputs, shrinking context of more than 40K tokens to about 1.6K. the KL dia token-level measure of visual dependence: vergence between the target models distributions with and without visual input, conditioned on the same textual prefix. Using this metric, we analyze two DFlash drafters for Qwen3.5-4B (Figure 3): the official text-trained drafter and counterpart trained on multimodal data following the official recipe. Acceptance rates decrease monotonically with visual dependence, from 46% in the lowest quartile to 22% in the highest. Moreover, the highest quartile accounts for 44% of first rejections within draft blocks, compared with only 7% for the lowest. This disparity persists after training with multimodal data. To address this challenge, we propose MMFlash (Figure 2), simple and effective framework for VLMs. Its core is visually aware loss reweighting scheme that uses the above visual dependence scores to emphasize visually dependent tokens in the DFlash cross-entropy objective. The additional weight scales with the drafters prediction error probability, emphasizing tokens it has yet to learn and gradually returning to the baseline weight as predictions improve. For long videos, drafter attention concentrates on nearby positions, with substantial redundancy among visual tokens. We thus equip the MMFlash drafter with simple sparse attention pattern that retains few attention sinks, strided visual tokens, all text tokens, and local window, consistently across training and inference. We evaluate MMFlash primarily on Qwen3.5 series [51] across seven image benchmarks covering text and document understanding, general VQA, and STEM reasoning, as well as three long video benchmarks (Figure 1). Baselines include native MTP, EAGLE-3, and DFlash. On image benchmarks, MMFlash achieves the longest average acceptance lengths and highest decoding speedups across all settings. Under greedy decoding, average speedups reach 3.00-3.05, exceeding DFlash by 10.3-10.9%. On long video benchmarks, sparse attention combined with minor video fine-tuning yields average speedups of 2.33-2.71, outperforming DFlash by 11.2-23.2%. MMFlash remains effective under high concurrency and generalizes to other model families and larger scales. Overall, we introduce MMFlash, novel diffusion drafting framework for speculative decoding in VLMs. By prioritizing poorly predicted, visually dependent tokens during training, MMFlash addresses key bottleneck in draft acceptance. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate its effectiveness and generalizability, establishing MMFlash as strong baseline for speculative decoding in VLMs. 2. Related Work We briefly review the most relevant work here and provide more detailed discussion in Appendix A. Speculative Decoding for VLMs. Speculative decoding [6, 34] lets lightweight drafter propose tokens that the target model verifies in parallel, leaving its output distribution unchanged and thus achieving lossless acceleration. Drafters range from decoding heads [5] to feature-level drafters with tree-structured verification [3739, 57]. For VLMs, existing methods differ mainly in how the drafter handles visual input: it receives the full visual input [17, 24, 41, 60], only distilled visual information [20, 26, 28, 30, 47, 76], or no visual tokens at all [16, 67, 74], and some methods switch among these strategies adaptively [21, 32, 33]. MMFlash follows the third and most efficient paradigm, since the target has already fused the visual content into the hidden states that the drafter reads. Orthogonal efforts relax 2 verification [27], speculate at the agent level [22], or specialize in document OCR [40]. Speculative Decoding with Diffusion Drafters. Diffusion language models (DLMs) [29, 50, 53, 56, 71, 78] generate text by denoising many positions in parallel, and block diffusion [3] applies this denoising within blocks that are generated autoregressively. Since DLM can propose whole block in one forward pass, early work explores diffusionstyle drafting by mixing diffusion and autoregressive objectives in one model [43], adapting autoregressive large language models (LLMs) for parallel drafting [54], or drafting with large pre-trained DLMs [35, 55]. DFlash [7] makes diffusion drafting simple and effective with lightweight drafter that emits an entire block in one forward pass, and follow-up work explores related designs [14, 23, 42] and dynamic position-wise loss weights [18, 65, 70]. 3. Preliminaries As baseline for our method, we briefly introduce DFlash [7], highlighting its inherent advantages for speculative decoding. Unlike autoregressive drafters, which require multiple sequential forward passes to propose draft tokens, DFlash generates an entire draft block in single forward pass. This parallelism decouples the number of sequential drafting passes from the number of draft tokens, allowing the computational budget otherwise spent on the drafting passes to support deeper, higher-capacity drafter. Concretely, at each drafting step, DFlash conditions on context features extracted from the target model and processes block of positions, one anchor token followed by 1 mask tokens, filling all masks in parallel. During training, anchors are randomly sampled from response generated by the target model, and the 1 tokens after each anchor are masked for reconstruction. This mirrors inference, where each block starts with the bonus token from the preceding verification step. Let denote the token that the target decoding policy selects at the k-th masked position, and let qk be the probability that the drafter assigns to it given the prefix. Training reduces to cross-entropy fit to the targets own choices, except that the 1 positions do not contribute equally to the loss: LDFlash = B1 (cid:88) k=1 (cid:0) log qk wk (cid:18) (cid:1), wk = exp (cid:19) , 1 γ where the hyperparameter γ > 0 sets how fast the weight decays along the block. This decay mirrors how block is consumed at inference time. Verification accepts prefix of the block, so rejection at position discards every token after it, and position lengthens the accepted sequence only when positions 1, . . . , 1 have all been accepted. 4. Method In this section, we first identify key limitation of extending DFlash to multimodal speculative decoding, which motivates us to propose our MMFlash. Then, we introduce our MMFlash in detail. 4.1. Motivation DFlash has been thoroughly validated in the text setting. Since our target is VLMs on multimodal data, the natural first question is how DFlash behaves on tokens that depend on the multimodal inputs (e.g., images). Answering it requires per-token measure of visual dependence, and we take this measure from the target model rather than from the drafter or from attention maps. For each generated token, we run the target model twice, once with the image and once with the image removed while keeping the text prompt and the generated prefix fixed, and define the tokens visual dependence as the KL divergence between the two resulting next-token distributions: = KL(cid:0)p( prefix, I) p( prefix)(cid:1), (1) where denotes the next-token distribution of the target model and the input image. This choice follows directly from how speculative decoding works. The sole objective of the drafter is to imitate the distribution of the target model, and draft token is accepted only when it matches the target models own prediction. What matters is therefore how much of the prediction that the drafter must reproduce is contributed by the image, which is exactly what the divergence above measures. Then, we conduct an empirical study on Qwen3.5-4B with two DFlash drafters: (1) the officially released drafter1, trained on text-only data; and (2) drafter we train following the official recipe on roughly 900K multimodal samples drawn from LLaVA-OV-1.5-Instruct-Data2. Every drafted token is scored by the visual dependence defined above and assigned to quartile from Q1 (least visual-dependent) to Q4 (most). We then report two statistics per quartile: the acceptance rate of drafted tokens; and the share of truncation points that fall in each quartile, where the truncation point of block is the first token at which the drafters prediction disagrees with the targets. As shown in Figure 3, across benchmarks and drafters the acceptance rate falls monotonically with visual dependence (46% in Q1 vs. 22% in Q4 on average, 2.1 gap), while truncation points pile up at the image-dependent end: Q4 holds 44% of them against 7% in Q1, and Q3-Q4 together account for 72-80%. The block-level view shows the same trend: block that opens on an image-dependent token retains far less of its draft, with acceptance falling from 33% in Q1 to 14% in Q4 on average (a 2.4 gap). Overall, these results indicate that the acceptance loss of DFlash on vision-language targets concentrates on visually dependent tokens and that training on multimodal data alone does not close this gap. This observation motivates MMFlash, which explicitly directs training toward such tokens rather than treating all positions alike. 4.2. MMFlash The study above shows where DFlash drafter loses its acceptance under the multimodal setting: on the tokens whose prediction the image decides. DFlashs objective is blind to this. Its weight wk depends only on the position inside block, so token that merely continues phrase and token that reads number off chart receive the same gradient. Yet the quantity that exposes the gap, the visual dependence d, is computed from the target alone, needs no drafter, and can be scored once offline for the training data. MMFlash therefore turns the diagnostic of Section 4.1 into training signal: it reweights the block loss so that the drafter spends its capacity where the image matters, and only while it has not yet learned those tokens. For every token of training response, we compute its visual dependence dt with Equation 1, i.e., with the target model, the image I, and the prefix x<t fixed. The score dt is precomputed once offline and stored with the training data, incurring no additional training cost. Following the analysis in Section 4.1, we likewise bucket the tokens in the training set by this score, and denote by gt [0, 1] the quantile of dt among all tokens in (see Appendix C.1 for details). Visual dependence tells us where the image matters; it does not tell us whether the target has settled on prediction there. The drafter is trained to reproduce the targets choice, and extra effort pays off only where there is definite choice to reproduce: on token whose with-image distribution is still flat, the target picks among near-tied candidates, and that pick is not predictable from its features no matter how the token is weighted. We therefore scale the score by the targets confidence with the image, measured by the entropy Ht of its with-image distribution p( x<t, I): gt = gt exp(Ht). We further examine video benchmarks, where the average input length increases from 477 tokens across seven image benchmarks to 41,218 tokens. Diffusion drafters such as DFlash attend to the entire target context at every drafting step, raising the question of whether fullcontext attention is necessary for small drafter. We therefore analyze the attention patterns of the trained MMFlash drafter on video inputs. Figure 4(a) shows that attention concentrates on the question and generated answer, while visual tokens receive diffuse attention with no frame standing out. Across 60 questions, Figure 4(b) confirms this locality: the most recent 256 positions account for only 0.8% of the context but receive 50.1% of the attention. In contrast, distant frames occupy over 96% of the context and collectively absorb 46% of the attention despite low attention per token, suggesting substantial redundancy in fullcontext drafting. Furthermore, we apply simple attention window to the trained MMFlash drafter. As shown in Figure 4(c), windowing reduces acceptance length on image benchmarks but improves it on video benchmarks, supporting the benefit of sparse attention in long video contexts. plain window discards visual evidence outside its range, potentially removing information needed to answer the question. Based on the observed attention patterns, we design simple sparse attention pattern specifically for video benchmarks. It retains the first 4 sink tokens, visual tokens sampled with stride of 32, all text tokens, and local window of 256 tokens. We use the same pattern during training and inference to ensure consistent context access. Implementation details are provided in Section 5.2. 5. Experiments 5.1. MMFlash therefore adaptively upweights these tokens while the drafter still predicts them poorly, and adopts sparse attention for long videos. It achieves the best average decoding speedups across seven image and three video benchmarks, remains effective under high serving concurrency, and generalizes to other model families, offering strong baseline for future work.

sections.title: Supplementary Material
sections.content: A. Extended Related Work Speculative Decoding for VLMs. Speculative decoding [5, 7, 34, 37] accelerates autoregressive generation by having lightweight draft model propose several candidate tokens that the target model verifies in single parallel forward pass, leaving the targets output distribution unchanged. Work has since pursued drafters that are cheaper yet better aligned with the target, ranging from auxiliary decoding heads [5] to feature-level drafting with treestructured verification [3739] and, most recently, drafters built on diffusion language models [7, 42]. Bringing speculative decoding to VLMs introduces design choice absent from the text-only setting: how the drafter should handle visual input. Existing methods fall into three paradigms according to this choice. The first exposes the drafter to the full visual input, strengthening its visual perception so as to raise the acceptance rate [17, 24, 41, 60]. The second supplies only distilled visual information, preserving the essential multimodal semantics while substantially reducing the drafters computation [20, 26, 28, 30, 47, 76]. The third, which this work adopts, removes visual tokens from the drafter altogether [16, 67, 74]. Since the target model has already fused the visual content into its hidden states during prefill, the drafter need not re-encode the visual input; its cost therefore no longer scales with the number of visual tokens, making this the fastest of the three paradigms. Rather than committing to single paradigm, several methods select the visual-input strategy adaptively at inference time according to the task at hand [21, 32, 33]. Orthogonal to the visualinput axis, other efforts relax the verification criterion to admit more draft tokens [27], lift speculation from the token level to the agent level [22], or tailor speculative decoding to vertical domains such as document OCR [40]. Speculative Decoding with Diffusion Drafters. Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) [50, 53, 71, 78] recast text generation as iterative denoising: starting from fully masked sequence, the model predicts every masked position in parallel and, over small number of refinement steps, commits to confident tokens while re-masking uncertain ones. Because generation is not bound to left-to-right order, dLLM can emit many tokens in single forward pass, offering test-time flexibility and efficiency that autoregressive decoding lacks, and recent large-scale DLMs achieve quality competitive with autoregressive LLMs [29, 50, 56]. Block diffusion [3] bridges the two families by running diffusion within fixed-size blocks that are themselves generated autoregressively, recovering KV caching and variablelength generation while retaining intra-block parallelism. These properties make DLMs natural drafters: whereas an autoregressive drafter spends one forward pass per token, DLM can propose whole block at once. Early explorations either blend the two paradigms within single model or retrofit autoregressive models for parallel drafting. Liu et al. [43] jointly trains diffusion and autoregressive objectives to think in parallel and talk sequentially, at the cost of exact losslessness, while Samragh et al. [54] exploit the future-token information implicitly encoded in autoregressive LLMs, adding LoRA adapter for parallel drafting and keeping the base model as verifier. DiffuSpec [35] and SpecDiff-2 [55] instead draft directly with large pretrained DLMs, relying on inference-time search or train test alignment to raise acceptance. DFlash [7] shows that the idea can be made simple and effective: lightweight diffusion drafter emits an entire block of candidates in one forward pass, which the target then verifies as in standard speculative decoding. Subsequent work refines this recipe: DART [42] pursues similar design; D-PACE [65] turns DFlashs fixed position-wise loss weights into dynamic schedule; Domino [23] adds causal dependencies within block so that later positions see earlier committed tokens rather than only masks; and Nemotron [14] unifies autoregressive, diffusion, and self-speculative decoding in single tri-mode model that drafts with diffusion and verifies autoregressively. F. Limitations & Future Work MMFlash is designed and evaluated for VLMs that take images or videos as input and generate text. For videos, it relies on simple sparse attention pattern and lightweight fine-tuning rather than drafter built specifically for video, and drafting on long videos remains harder than on images. promising direction is therefore to tailor speculative decoding to videos, for example by selecting the drafters visual context according to the question, compressing the redundancy across frames, and measuring visual dependence at the frame level so that training focuses on tokens grounded in specific moments. Another direction is to extend MMFlash to omni-modal models [59, 68], which also take audio as input and generate streaming speech. This would require generalizing visual dependence to tokens that depend on audio or on joint audio-visual cues, handling even longer interleaved audio-visual contexts, and accelerating speech generation in addition to text.
